question: Should guided option selection become eligible for a narrow English policy probe with these guardrails, or stay deferred/rewrite first?
example_context: Example product only: a $29 subscription and a $59 subscription. These examples are review candidates, not approved runtime copy.

examples.title: Two-option choice
examples.customer_turn: So do I choose the $29 option or the $59 option?
examples.proposed_response: There are two fair paths: $29 for the basics, or $59 for more included. Which feels closer to what you'd actually use? Neither is fine too.
examples.review_question: Does this let the customer choose without making one option feel mandatory?
examples.risk: The agent could sound like it is steering toward a plan while pretending the customer created the idea.

examples.title: Fit is unclear
examples.customer_turn: I can see both paths, I am just not sure which one fits me.
examples.proposed_response: Start with use, not pressure: $29 if basics are enough, $59 if you want more included. Which side fits better, or should we pause?
examples.review_question: Is this low-pressure enough, or does it still push the customer toward choosing today?
examples.risk: A choice frame can collapse uncertainty into a sale attempt too early.

examples.title: Recommendation request
examples.customer_turn: Which route would you suggest for someone like me?
examples.proposed_response: I shouldn't choose for you. I can make the tradeoff clear: $29 is the lighter start, $59 has more included. Which sounds closer?
examples.review_question: Should the agent refuse to choose for the customer before offering the two-option frame?
examples.risk: Direct recommendation language can become advice or authority pressure.

examples.title: Difference first
examples.customer_turn: What is the real difference between the $29 option and the $59 option?
examples.proposed_response: I can explain the difference first. $29 is the lower starting point; $59 includes more. No payment details needed.
examples.review_question: Is this an acceptable bridge when the customer wants explanation before choosing?
examples.risk: The runtime must not invent exact feature differences beyond approved product facts.

examples.title: Not now
examples.customer_turn: Can I choose later instead of deciding on this call?
examples.proposed_response: Yes. Not now is a valid answer. I can leave both options open and send the $29/$59 difference in writing.
examples.review_question: Does this preserve autonomy clearly enough?
examples.risk: The agent must not treat deferral as hidden consent to continue selling.

examples.title: Neither option
examples.customer_turn: I'm not sure either is right.
examples.proposed_response: Then neither may be the right answer today. We can pause, or just compare what each option includes.
examples.review_question: Should this be the default fallback when neither option feels right?
examples.risk: A guided option tactic must keep a real non-sale path available.

examples.title: Payment boundary
examples.customer_turn: If I pick one, can I pay now?
examples.proposed_response: No payment details needed. This review is only about whether either option is worth considering.
examples.review_question: Should payment stay blocked even when a customer chooses an option?
examples.risk: Option selection must not become checkout, card collection, or contract signing.
